title: Subscription Traps: How Free Trials Make Billions

beats.say: Meet Jess. She signs up for a free seven day trial of a streaming service. Just to watch one show. She tells herself she'll cancel before it ends.
You see, three months later, Jess is still paying, every month, for something she hasn't opened since that first week.
Jess isn't alone. The UK government has estimated that there are nearly ten million unwanted subscriptions in the UK, costing consumers around one point six billion pounds a year.

vis.text: £1.6 billion a year on unwanted subscriptions.

beats.say: It's not just streaming. Apps, gyms, meal kits, magazines, software, cloud storage, delivery passes and dating apps all use subscriptions. Some offer cheap first months that jump in price later.
Nearly ten million subscriptions that people don't really want, still being paid for.

vis.label: million unwanted subscriptions in the UK, nearly

beats.say: Part one. Why free trials work.
Free trials are brilliant for companies. They get you to hand over your card details when you're excited and the cost feels like zero. Then they rely on one simple fact. People forget.
For a company, a subscriber who forgets is incredibly profitable. They pay every month, but cost almost nothing to serve, because they never use the service.

vis.text: A forgotten subscriber is pure profit.

beats.say: Psychologists talk about inertia. Once something is set up, doing nothing is the easiest option. Cancelling takes effort. So many people just carry on, even when they don't want the service.
Part two. The tricks.
Some companies make signing up take one click, but cancelling take ages. Hidden menus. Phone calls only. Pages asking, are you sure? three times. These are sometimes called dark patterns.
Regulators have taken action against some firms. And consumer groups have repeatedly called out companies for making cancellation needlessly hard.

vis.text: Regulators and consumer groups are watching.

beats.say: Common tricks include automatically renewing at a higher price after a discount ends, small charges that are easy to miss on a bank statement, and annual renewals that come round when you've forgotten all about them.
A few pounds a month doesn't feel like much. But add up a few subscriptions you don't use, and it can easily be hundreds of pounds a year.
Jess checked her statement. A music app. A fitness app. A cloud storage plan. And that streaming service. She'd forgotten about most of them.

cast.say: Four subscriptions? I only remember one!

beats.say: Part three. The new rules.
The government is bringing in new rules to tackle subscription traps, under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act. They're expected to take effect in spring twenty twenty seven.

Under the new rules, businesses will have to send reminders before a free trial ends or a subscription renews. Cancelling will have to be straightforward. And there'll be cooling off periods, so people can cancel and get a refund after a trial rolls into a paid subscription.
Businesses will also have to give clear information before you sign up, including how much you'll pay after the trial, and how to cancel.

vis.text: Clear information before you sign up.

beats.say: Until those rules are in force, the responsibility is mostly on you. So here's how to protect yourself.
Part four. How to protect yourself.
When Jess signs up for a free trial now, she sets a reminder on her phone for a couple of days before it ends. Some services even let you cancel straight away and still keep the free trial.

cast.say: Reminder set. Trial cancelled. Still free!

beats.say: Every few months, go through your bank and card statements and look for regular payments. Ask yourself, have I used this in the last month? If not, cancel it. You can always sign up again later.

vis.title: The subscription audit
items: Used it in the last month?

beats.say: Some banking apps show all your subscriptions in one place, and some let you block payments to specific companies. You can also use a separate card for subscriptions, so they're easy to track.
And watch out for annual subscriptions. They can be good value, but they renew for a big lump sum, often when you've forgotten. Put the renewal date in your calendar.

vis.text: Annual renewals can be a nasty surprise.

beats.say: Jess cancelled three subscriptions she'd forgotten about. That's more than two hundred pounds a year back in her pocket.
Free trials aren't evil. They can be a good way to try something. But the business model often depends on you forgetting. So don't forget.

vis.text: The model depends on you forgetting.

beats.say: Subscribe, this is one subscription you can keep, and tell me in the comments which subscription you forgot to cancel.
